title: Portraiture as a research method: Sara Lawrence-Lightfoot's "painting with words", how it differs from ethnography, and the case against it
dek: Portraiture puts the researcher's own judgement at the centre of a study and measures success by whether readers recognise the truth of the portrait, not by whether anyone could repeat it. Its sharpest critic says that leaves no way to check the portraitist; its founder's answer is that a visible self demands more discipline, not less.

title: How investigative YouTube video essays are built: the cold open, the late turn to meaning, and the channels that borrow the form without the evidence
dek: The strongest forensic video essays open on an artifact, walk through evidence in the order a viewer would experience it, and say what it all means only late in the video. That delayed turn is what persuades, which is why the same structure works just as well for channels whose evidence does not hold up.

title: Paying to reach curious readers in 2026: ChatGPT ads, feed ads, paid newsletter recommendations, and the labelling rules
dek: ChatGPT now sells self-serve ads, but they cost about 3–8× more per impression than feed ads and are hard to measure, so the cheapest curious readers are still on Meta and Reddit. An ad can be the whole useful answer and still carry its label: the rules draw the line at fake people and hidden sponsors, not at ads that are worth reading.

title: How Canada's public-sector employees vote: the Canadian Election Study evidence, Ottawa's ridings, and the union endorsements
dek: Public-sector workers in Canada lean modestly left of private-sector workers, and most of that lean belongs to unionized professionals and managers. The city crews whose unions endorse the NDP vote much like their private-sector counterparts, and no released poll gives a party-by-party split to settle it.

title: Paying yourself to do your own tasks: what the incentive trials show, and whether an earn-back subscription could work
dek: Financial incentives move behaviour while they run, and losses move people more than equal gains. Paying yourself a wage from your own pocket removes most of what the trials rely on; a subscription you earn back by doing the work is a loss-framed stake, and the research rates it the version most likely to work. Nobody has tested it.

title: Canadian recessions and the mortgage channel: rate decisions, CMHC, and five decades of housing-led downturns
dek: Every major Canadian downturn since 1980 carries a monetary-policy fingerprint, and housing is how the decision reaches people. The clearest case is 1990, where the campaign overshot its own target and Toronto prices did not pass their 1989 peak until 2002.

title: Temporary foreign workers and Canadian innovation: what the automation evidence shows, and the study nobody has run
dek: The research that says immigration drives innovation studies points-selected skilled migration. Canada's intake since 2016 has been mostly temporary and low-wage, and the causal work on cheap labour runs the other way — a 1% rise in low-skill wages lifts automation patenting 2–5%. The Canadian version of that study has never been done.

title: Whey protein in hot black coffee: why it curdles, what the heat-stable versions cost, and what is coming
dek: Collagen disappears into a hot cup; whey turns it into pale lumps that smell of sulfur. Coffee's acidity sits almost exactly where whey is least stable, and it is served above the temperature that unfolds the protein. The heat-stable ingredients that exist solve it by cutting the protein up, which makes it bitter.

title: Bill C-11 and Canadian creators in 2026: what the CRTC has actually imposed, and what is still a prediction
dek: Creators were told the Online Streaming Act would cost them their foreign audiences by teaching recommendation systems that Canadian videos go unwatched. Three years after royal assent the regulator has imposed no discoverability requirement on anyone, the money is stayed by a court, and no study has measured the harm.

title: Topping up low wages in Canada: the Canada Workers Benefit, employer capture, and the workers who never file
dek: Canada already runs the alternative to a basic income — a refundable credit that tops up low earnings automatically. Two things decide whether it works: employers absorb part of any wage subsidy where no floor exists, and about 9% of eligible earners never file a return.

title: How YouTube, Instagram and TikTok rank video in 2026: satisfaction signals, AI content understanding, and penalties for reposting
dek: Recommendation feeds have stopped scoring behaviour alone. A language model now watches the content and judges it — better than the crowd-sourced raters it replaced — while reposting is penalised in the ranking itself. Much of what creators are taught describes the system of a decade ago.

title: Measuring the economy with new instruments: scraped prices, card-spending trackers and satellite imagery
dek: Four old arguments explain why an economy resists being computed, and none of them have gone away. What computation did change is measurement — scraped prices, card records and satellite images that report what is happening weeks before the official numbers do.

title: Immigrants, temporary residents and Canada's job growth since 2020: what the Labour Force Survey can and cannot show
dek: Nearly all of Canada's post-pandemic job growth went to immigrants and temporary residents. But no Canadian government table publishes that split the way the American one does — every version of the figure is built by hand from an annual series that undercounts the very group it counts.

title: Missed workouts and broken streaks: how fast strength, mood and habit actually decay
dek: Two weeks away from the gym costs almost nothing in muscle — strength holds and the body keeps a record that makes the regain fast. What drains in that time is mood, dopamine tone and the automatic habit, which is exactly what restarting runs on.

title: Alcohol blackouts: how ethanol blocks memory formation, and why drinking speed decides it
dek: In an alcohol blackout the drinker is awake, talking and deciding, while the brain's ability to save the night is chemically held shut. Nothing comes back afterwards because nothing was stored — and how fast the drinking goes decides whether it happens at all.

title: Fred Hutch's HSV gene therapy in 2026: mouse and guinea-pig results, no human trial, and the antivirals arriving first
dek: A gene therapy clears up to 97% of dormant herpes in mice. In the animal that relapses the way people do it clears above 30%, nobody has filed to test it in a person, and the drugs arriving first suppress the virus rather than remove it.

title: Job guarantees in Austria, France and India: employment effects, cost per job, and the designs that trap people
dek: A job for anyone who wants one sounds utopian. It has been tried — in an Austrian town, in 83 French territories and across rural India. It works, it costs money, and the design decides whether it is a springboard or a trap.

title: Language models and idea diversity: homogenisation within a session, across users, and between companies
dek: Ask a language model for something new and it pulls toward what everyone else would say — across companies, over long sessions, and across everyone using it. Real novelty has a shape the models do not reach for on their own.

title: Opioid deaths and overdose calls in Hamilton: why the two counts moved in opposite directions
dek: Hamilton's opioid deaths have fallen every year since 2021, while paramedic calls for overdoses more than doubled. The death count is measuring a drug supply that no longer exists.

title: Canada's short-term rental rules: supply, prices, and the mid-term rental tier that never formed
dek: Short-term rentals add flexible supply, and competition lowers prices. Canadian cities banned them anyway — and cut off a tier between a hotel and a lease just as it was forming.

title: Canada's short-term rental bans and rents: what returned to the long-term market, and what actually moved prices
dek: Canadian cities restricted short-term rentals to bring homes back to renters. Few came back, rents fell for other reasons, and the bans squeezed a new kind of housing that sits between a hotel and a lease.

title: The visual detour
dek: The internet from about 1990 to 2022 as a fifty-year swing back toward print — screens of text and keyboards — inside the longer return to speech that McLuhan predicted, now ending as voice interfaces take over.

title: Where does speaking start to beat typing?
dek: There is no established academic literature using the specific term "friction threshold" for voice.

title: Does naming a feeling work the way McLuhan said language works?
dek: Based on this search pass: no published work explicitly bridges McLuhan's medium-of-media theory of language to either Lieberman's affect-labeling neuroscience or Barkley/Vygotsky inner-speech theory.

title: Can the tetrad forecast what AI turns into?
dek: The tetrad has been little applied to the major artifacts of the present: large language models, recommender systems, the smartphone-plus-app stack, cryptocurrency, the cloud, augmented reality.

title: Would a legal tier between a hotel and a lease lower rents?
dek: There is no public Hamilton-specific data on the MTR share of its 1,250 units, but the broader Canadian pattern would suggest the market was structurally changing — not just returning to its 2019 form.

title: The in-between rental
dek: A thought experiment: a legal, recognised tier for stays of one to three months — furnished, flexible, taxed by price rather than capped by nights — between a hotel room and a year-long lease.

title: Do firms that rely on temporary workers innovate less?
dek: There is no published study directly comparing innovation output between TFW-heavy and TFW-light Canadian firms or industries.

title: How do public-sector workers vote, party by party?
dek: There is, however, no publicly released Canadian poll that breaks down decided‑voter support by employment sector with the kind of "X% Liberal / Y% Conservative / Z% NDP" topline that exists for, say, gender or age.

title: What happens to the buildings Canada pays for abroad?
dek: There is no separate, transparent disclosure of how Canada's foreign-built assets are treated in current public reporting — this is a gap.

title: Does the journalism tax credit change what outlets say?
dek: No publicly available study has yet attempted a quantitative content analysis correlating outlet-level CJLTC dollars and editorial tone.

title: Why people keep scrolling: habit, infinite feeds, and the evidence against the dopamine explanation
dek: The best evidence says people keep scrolling because of habit and a feed that never ends — not because of a dopamine jackpot. And engagement-ranked feeds keep showing people what they say they do not want.

title: Unverified hunches in AI-assisted software work: the certainty handoff and one-sided memory
dek: A hunch that feels right gets handed to a collaborator as if it had been checked. When the collaborator is an AI that starts every session blank, nobody checks it at all.

title: Does a daily digest beat an endless feed?
dek: No peer-reviewed study I found directly tests a daily digest.

title: Does toe spacing predict skin that keeps cracking?
dek: I found no study directly measuring toe-spacing anatomy as a predictor of recurrent interdigital xerosis.

title: Can compounds from HIV cure research wake latent herpes?
dek: PKC-agonist plant diterpenes are the most promising untested transfer from HIV cure research.

title: Did the text-internet generation think differently from the video one?
dek: No study compares a typographic-internet cohort with a video-internet cohort.

title: Does better proof make advertisers pay more?
dek: I found no published evidence that newsletter advertisers pay more or rebook more with better proof.

title: Do “save for later” flows work for creator links?
dek: I found no published study of save-for-later, send-to-device or reminder flows for creator-referred traffic.

title: Do AI-voiced ad reads work as well as human ones?
dek: I found no rigorous public evidence that synthetic host-reads perform as well as human reads.

title: Does a creator’s recommendation change what an AI agent recommends?
dek: I found no controlled study isolating a creator's recommendation as the cause of an agent recommendation.

title: Will an AI agent ever weigh a signed receipt?
dek: I found no agent that treats a user-held code or signed receipt as a ranking or attribution input.

title: Do creators want a portable record of their recommendations?
dek: This pass found no survey asking creators whether they want a portable record of their endorsements, and no product that sells portability as a paid add-on.

title: Does offering “keep it for later” at the click raise revenue?
dek: Nobody has published a test of the specific claim, that offering "keep it" at the click raises credited revenue over 60–90 days.

title: What does an extra email step cost in clicks?
dek: No study found measures what an optional email step costs in click-through to an affiliate merchant.

title: Does on-site AI chat actually lift sales?
dek: I found no independent controlled experiment of on-site AI chat lift this pass.

title: Can sound carry the story in a data documentary?
dek: Nobody has shipped a linear documentary that treats sonification as a first-class, frame-synced narrative device (as opposed to accessibility add-on or standalone art).

title: Do the extras in collagen supplements add anything?
dek: No RCT compares collagen + cofactors vs collagen alone.

title: Is RealPage-style rent software being used in Canada?
dek: I found no equivalent enforcement action — a genuine open question

title: How common is algorithmic price collusion in real markets?
dek: Calvano et al. is robust experimentally; real-world prevalence and detectability remain open.

title: Krasis
dek: The synthesis of the series. McLuhan said every medium changes the ratio among our senses; the paper series tests that literally, from ADHD and typing to drugs and addiction, and find one configuration that media, drugs and illness all re-temper.

title: Exocrasis
dek: The computing environment, not the screen, is the medium: keyboard, memory, search and network move part of the configuration of the senses and of memory outside the body.

title: Heterocrasis
dek: ADHD as a different starting balance of the senses. The strongest difference is in overall gain; the body and inner speech are mixed; binding is not looser.

title: Pharmakrasis
dek: Each class of drug sets its own balance of the senses — and the evidence for that is better than for any medium. When a drug meets a medium, as music does in psychedelic therapy, the two make a third thing.

title: Narcocrasis
dek: In dependence, what goes unseen is not the drug but the shifted baseline: the allostatic state is the medium, the drug its content. Two routes back — one turns the gain down, one makes the ground visible.

title: Narcocrasis
dek: In drug dependence, the part a person stops noticing is not the drug but their own shifted baseline: flatter pleasures, a restless body, a raised stress tone. The drug feels like the fix; the changed baseline feels like how the world is.

title: Anacrasis
dek: Recovery as re-setting that baseline, not only removing the drug. The ancient Greek word anakrasis meant mixing with others, and the evidence points the same way: what helps the reset last is other people.

title: Pharmakrasis
dek: Every class of drug sets its own characteristic balance of the senses: cannabis speeds felt time, ketamine loosens the sense of owning a body, LSD deepens the response to music. A drug, on this view, is a technology of the senses, like a medium but more direct.

title: Heterocrasis
dek: People start from different balances of the senses before any medium touches them. ADHD may be one such starting point, most clearly in how loudly the brain turns all its signals up or down.

title: Exocrasis
dek: Part of how we sense and remember now lives outside the body, in keyboards, search, saved files and the network. The computing environment holds some of the balance the brain used to hold.

title: Fixed times versus flexible routines in exercise habits: what the paid-to-exercise trials found
dek: Paid to exercise at a set time, people did less than those paid to exercise whenever they liked — and quit faster afterwards. What helps is a fixed start and an open workout.

title: Typomora
dek: McLuhan said electric media would bring back the voice. For fifty years computers made us type instead. The delay was the keyboard, not a mistake in the theory — and it is ending.

title: Sensory syncrasis
dek: McLuhan meant his "sense ratios" literally. The brain science he reached for failed; predictive processing now gives the idea a mechanism, a name and five tests.

title: Self-extinguishing maintenance: treatments that stop because they are working, and the relapse that follows
dek: Some problems only stay fixed while you keep treating them — a gap between two teeth, toes pressed too tight. The treatment works, the problem vanishes, it looks cured, you stop, and it comes back. This research named the cycle and the mistake behind it.

title: Typomora: Neuroscience, Naming and Framing for Paper 3
dek: The neuroscience: Literacy measurably changes the brain. Dehaene et al. (2010, Science) found increased responses to letters in the visual word form area (VWFA), a small displacement of face responses, and enhanced…

title: The Computing Environment and Sensory Syncrasis: Evidence Review for Paper 2
dek: What the environment tunes toward: an outward-facing, fast-switching, offloaded mode. Readers calibrate less carefully and process expository text more shallowly on screens (g ≈ −0.21). Memory shifts toward external stores…

title: Sensory Syncrasis Evidence Base: Screens (Paper A) and ADHD (Paper B)
dek: Paper A (Screens): Change is real but mostly domain-specific and often enhancing. Action video games causally improve perceptual and attentional skills (Bediou et al. 2018: g = 0.34 in intervention studies, g = 0.55…

title: The Precision Ratio, Revisited: Why "Ratio" Is Half Right, and What to Call the Whole
dek: Naming study

title: The Medium Becomes the Ground: McLuhan and the Allostatic Model of Addiction (rebuilt)
dek: Work linking McLuhan to drugs and addiction exists only at the level of discourse and metaphor. The nearest example is Hartogsohn & Vudka (2023, Transcultural Psychiatry), which is about smartphone "addiction" and McLuhan's…

title: Sensory syncrasis
dek: The whole configuration of how the brain blends its senses: how much it trusts each one, how loud it turns them all, whether it fuses or separates them, the balance between body and world, and how long a setting lasts. From the Greek root of idiosyncrasy.

title: Typomora
dek: The typed delay in McLuhan's predicted return to voice: fifty years in which the keyboard, not the medium, kept networked communication typographic. Typos, type, and mora, delay — also the unit of spoken time.

title: Epanaphony
dek: The return of voice as the way we put language into machines — dictation, voice notes, talking to AI — that closes the typomora. Oral in production, typographic in storage.

title: Does talking to an AI change how you think?
dek: No peer-reviewed study tests how voice conversation with an AI affects memory, composition or thinking. The one widely cited study of AI and thinking was typed, and is an unreviewed preprint.

title: Does typing weaken speaking?
dek: No study shows that heavy typing degrades speech production, or that heavy speaking improves typed composition. Whether practice in one carries over to the other is untested.

title: Does dictation train speech?
dek: No peer-reviewed study shows that dictation or speech-to-text improves unaided spoken fluency or confidence. Speech-recognition feedback does improve pronunciation, which makes it a testable idea.

title: Do screens shift the balance of the senses?
dek: Nobody has measured whether what children watch or play changes which sense dominates when sight and sound compete — the closest measurable form of McLuhan's sense ratio.

title: Inner speech in ADHD
dek: No study had looked specifically at inner speech in ADHD as of a 2015 review, and no study has tested whether naming a feeling calms it less in ADHD.

title: The Medium Becomes the Ground: Foundation Research on Sense Ratios, Precision, Interoception, Allostasis and Addiction
dek: Historiography: McLuhan stated in physiological terms that media "alter sense ratios or patterns of perception steadily and without any resistance," funded and ran media-comparison experiments in the 1950s, and in…

title: Personalised pricing software and the return of haggling, run from the seller's side
dek: From the middle of the nineteenth century everyone paid the number on the tag. Pricing software is bringing the bazaar back — except this time the seller reads you, and you see nothing.

title: The price as instruction
dek: A price computed for one buyer from their data, rather than posted for everyone — the same number, carrying the seller's model of you instead of the market's signal. Extends Gardiner Means's “administered prices” (1930s) from the boardroom to the shopper.

title: What influenced the AI's purchase?
dek: No AI company reports which pages or sources shaped what its shopping assistant bought, in a form anyone else can check. Until one does, nobody outside it can measure an ad's effect on an AI buyer.

title: Does the same basket cost more on your phone?
dek: Nobody has measured whether online prices in Canada change with your location, device or history. The US has a federal study; Canada has little enforcement and almost no documentation.

title: The infinite-scroll trial nobody ran
dek: No randomised trial compares infinite scroll with pagination on time spent or wellbeing. One review of the evidence says it looked and found none.

title: Rework from unchecked hunches
dek: No study measures how much rework comes from unverified human intuitions handed to coding agents — the link the record's first article leans on.

title: Books kept on the publisher's side
dek: No product lets a publisher set the influence it had against the credit it was paid. Merchant tools suggest codes and links catch 15–30% of conversions, but that data belongs to brands.

title: A referral that survives a remix
dek: Of eleven products checked, only Framer documents a referral parameter that carries through a remix, duplicate or template link. Everywhere else the credit is lost at the copy.

title: Timing antivirals to the body clock
dek: Clock genes change how HSV enters cells in the lab. Whether dosing antivirals by circadian phase helps people has not been tested.

title: A tax on money that sits still
dek: No one has seriously built a Pigouvian tax on hoarded, immobile capital. The closest precedent is demurrage — a fee for holding currency.

title: Who will count an AI assistant's influence: advertising attribution after the agent
dek: Every shift in how advertising is paid for happened when a new party could count a new event. The agent that now does the buying can count the one that matters — and reports it to no one.

title: The counter-irritant spiral: McLuhan, Hans Selye, and relief that deepens the need for relief
dek: In 1964 McLuhan, reading the stress researcher Hans Selye, described relief that deepens the need for relief "like a drug habit." What users stop noticing is not the drug but their own shifted baseline.

title: Uber for Your Own To-Do List: Feasibility and Prior-Art Review of a Paid, AI-Dispatched Task Queue
dek: Prior art: Nobody has built "Uber for your own tasks". The nearby products are commitment-stake apps (Beeminder, stickK, Forfeit), pay-for-health apps (Sweatcoin, Evidation), RPG and gamified task managers (Habitica, Finch)…

sub: Evidence only · the case is held
title: Time Blindness, Task-Hopping, and Why a Delivery Queue Feels Easy
dek: "Time blindness" is a popular term, not a diagnosis. Large meta-analyses find that people with ADHD judge time intervals less accurately and less consistently. The best-known pooled result is Metcalfe et al. (2024), with…

title: Cash micro-incentives for task completion in adults with ADHD
dek: No randomised trial tests whether small, immediate payments move task completion in adults with ADHD. The one adaptive-incentive study (Lee et al. 2023) was null. Open until a document reports a trial.

title: Attenuate
dek: A task app for executive dysfunction: one task at a time, dispatched like a delivery order, with small rewards for finishing.

title: Self-extinguishing maintenance
dek: A routine that works so well it removes the thing that made you do it — so it stops, and the problem comes back.

title: CPAI — cost per attested influence
dek: Paying for a verifiable role in an AI agent’s choice, rather than for a click or a sale.

title: The agent as overhearer
dek: An AI agent that only hears the instruction, not the conversation that produced it.

title: Ancaster
dek: Eighteen research passes toward a publisher-owned layer that lets a reader keep a recommendation and come back to it without the recommender losing credit.

title: Whey protein that dissolves in hot black coffee
dek: Nobody sells a protein powder that dissolves cleanly in hot black coffee.

dek: No competitor sells proof. Paved, Passionfroot, beehiiv, EthicalAds and SponsorCal report clicks, opens, impressions and reviews at best. I found no creator or newsletter marketplace offering holdout lift, verified…

dek: Build it from public content, verify it with OAuth, and never blur the two. YouTube's Analytics API gives consented age, gender, geography and traffic-source data. Its June 2026 derived-metrics amendment allows custom scores…

dek: Owning the redirect is worth something, but not for conversion. Its real value is maintenance and evidence. Old links rot and programs change: Amazon cut commissions again in 2026, by as much as 50% according to Adweek, and…

dek: Frontier #1 (agents) matters most, and it changes the pass-six plan. Profound's tracking found feed-sourced ChatGPT picks jumping from 8.26% to 61.54% on 10 July 2026. OpenAI retired in-chat Instant Checkout in March 2026.…

dek: Across five decades, Canada's recessions are not random market accidents but are repeatedly detonated by identifiable policy decisions — above all Bank of Canada interest-rate cycles acting on an economy where housing and…

dek: The lead thesis is sound and publishable: for two centuries the price was understood as an emergent signal no one sets (Hayek, 1945); algorithmic, dynamic, and surveillance pricing increasingly make the price computed and…

dek: The genuine Canadian story is forensic-historical, not live: algorithmic revenue-management software (RealPage's YieldStar/AIRM/LRO; Yardi's Revenue IQ/RENTmaximizer) was used here from at least 2017, grew gradually, then…

dek: NDM has never been applied to directing coding agents.

dek: No natural compound has been shown to destroy or eradicate HSV latency in human neurons.

dek: TEWL that track the omega-3 index; pure fish-oil RCTs mostly measure UV/inflammation, not wrinkles, and EPA appears more potent than DHA in skin but no head-to-head wrinkle trial exists.

dek: Fenwick English (2000)—for the unchecked authority of the single "truth-telling" portraitist, its pursuit of an "essence," and the difficulty of independently verifying its claims.
